cim: Art and artificial intelligence stand side by side in the halls
cim_eredeti: Art and artificial intelligence stand side by side in the halls
szoveg_eredeti:
While Wando has much to offer when it comes to student life, the roster of clubs has forever been a huge student draw. Throughout the years as clubs have come and gone, but there have been a small few that have been running for years on end. One of these was Art Club, until its abrupt disbandment earlier this school year.

The school now offers after-school art classes where teachers are paid to instruct them, and to the surprise of many Art Club patrons, like president and senior member Payton Walker, these classes will be taking the place of what used to be Art Club.

“[The school] moved towards the art classes … because of funding, and it’s mostly controlled through … the district. … It’s a lot on the teacher to stay after school and they don’t get paid as much and they also have families. But also, the fact that it’s run mostly through the district makes me feel a little ignored because it’s part of … a district that doesn’t know anything about how our club is at Wando and is placing all these rules and regulations,” Walker said.

The National Art Honors Society (NAHS) board was informed of this change at their first yearly meeting, and it was not met with a positive reaction.

“It kind of told us that we were obsolete, because they had figured everything out without us, and we had to kind of go talk to [Media Arts teacher Anna] Kamoroff, who had come up with a new idea for Art Club, and we kind of fought for the same Art Club that we had last year,” Walker said.

With the new school year, there has been an influx of artificial intelligence-generated posters and fliers in the school hallway, on the school website, and on school-affiliated social media. One of the new Art Club’s goals this school year is to offer a place for organizations and clubs to source student-made posters.

“It just kind of feels very impersonal. It feels lazy, and it also feels like when other clubs or student organizations use AI to create a poster, they’re kind of ignoring all of the life that we have at Wando High School, and the students who would love to do stuff like that, and it kind of shows how certain [organizations] don’t really think about student involvement or don’t really care about the students,” Walker said.

One of the organizations at the front of the AI conversation has been the Parent Teacher Student Organization (PTSO). After posting a slideshow of AI-generated images detailing Wando in 1980s attire, some students were quick to react and express their discomfort.

“AI is clearly here to stay, just as other forms of digital editing and content creation, from Snapchat filters to Canva tools and everything in between, have become part of everyday social media. We also fully understand that there are appropriate and inappropriate uses of AI, particularly in an academic setting, and we think those distinctions matter. From the PTSO perspective, our social media is meant to be fun, engaging and supportive of the Wando community,” Harris wrote.

But the PTSO is not the only organization using generative AI. Student Council has also used it occasionally to make social media posts and school flyers. Adviser Casey Woronowich explained that, in time crunches, the tool can often come in handy.

“I think there were some students upset because they were asking about like, ‘Oh, well there are plenty of … artists that can do it,’ but we’ve already asked the artists to come in and to help with the stuff,” Woronowich said. “We’ve reached out to the people in the art classes to see if they wanted to help out and do any of the fliers, and nobody has the time to do so.”

Following a social media post of hers criticizing the PTSO for its AI usage, senior Stella Merreighn met with Woronowich in the student council room. Merreighn received an email from Woronowich, and got together to discuss how she and other students can help the Student Council with graphics. Merreighn said that she was free to help anytime and was only an email away.

“I told her [that] and she hasn’t emailed me at all. … There are so many people … [that] would be happy to have their work on display, but just the fact that they’re just ignoring all of the students that would probably want to do this … makes me mad,” Merreighn said.

Student media advisor Phillip Caston works with plenty of student artists daily, yet even he surrenders to generative AI on occasion.

“[For Sports Marketing, what] we use is … basically just backgrounds and fonts. … We still maintain the integrity of the photos that are … shot by the Wando Photography Department,” Caston said. “Even though the Sports Marketing [Program] is a subsidiary of Tribal Tribune that serves as a promotional entity for the athletic department. … We don’t let that trickle into the journalistic part because we still have to maintain, you know, completely student-original work while producing the newsmagazine or the online newspaper.”

What most parties agree on, is that at the end of the day the discussion of generative AI use is not a completely black and white issue.

“I would encourage [students] to be curious and find out why it’s being used. … It could be that an organization needs help and they could be the ones who … bring that help. … But also just to be empathetic and understand … why it’s maybe being used and what context is being used [in],” Caston said.
